title: Biological Invasions and the Reconfiguration of Global Biogeographical Patterns
content:
ABSTRACT

Aim

Biological invasions are redistributing species across the planet, yet their consequences for the spatial patterns that structure biodiversity remain poorly resolved. Here, we synthesise empirical evidence to evaluate how human-mediated species introductions are reshaping the core biogeographical rules that describe the geography of life on Earth.

Location

Global, covering terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems.

Time Period

Contemporary (20th–21st centuries), corresponding to the acceleration of biological invasions under globalisation.

Major Taxa Studied

Plants, vertebrates, and invertebrates; with additional evidence from other taxa where available.

Methods

We performed a systematic review of the literature across major biogeographical patterns, including latitudinal diversity gradients, biogeographical regionalisation, species–area and diversity–isolation relationships, Bergmann's and Rapoport's ecogeographical rules and range-size distributions. Searches in Web of Science and Google Scholar identified 2652 records, of which 150 publications met inclusion criteria. Records were classified by ecological unit, taxon, ecosystem, spatial scale, outcome relative to rule expectations, effect pathway, and explanatory driver.

Results

Biological invasions are substantially altering global biodiversity patterns. Several long-standing relationships, such as the delineation of global biogeographical regions, island diversity–isolation gradients, and Bergmann's Rule, are already fundamentally reshaped. Others, including species-area relationships and range-size distributions, are reinforced or remain consistent with classical expectations. Effects are strongest at broad spatial scales and in highly invaded systems, particularly islands and temperate regions. Across rules, outcomes were driven mainly by spatial variation in colonisation and propagule pressure, with additional relevant roles for environmental filtering and temporal dynamics.

Main Conclusions

Biological invasions are redefining the geography of life in the Anthropocene. While some biogeographical regularities persist, others are being weakened or replaced by novel human-driven patterns. This selective reorganisation points to a shift from biogeography structured primarily by dispersal limitation, environmental filtering, and evolutionary history toward one increasingly shaped by anthropogenic transport, introduction history, and invasion pressure.
